svg.text: Washing machine meets concrete mixer meets wok: one stainless drum spins 5–900 rpm and tilts mouth-up to mouth-down.
drum Ø 300 × 350, cup on a rear shaft
self-wash 6 L, 9 min, then 110 °C by its own coil
pot / pan / dish on hob or shuttle
Speed decides what the drum does
critical speed of a Ø 300 drum: 42.3 / √0.3 = 77 rpm
20–30 rpm mix, coat · 45–55 rpm wash, peel
above 77 rpm: pinned to the wall
450 rpm = 34 g: spin-dry, throw off water
Loose liners (no permanent gap): bare drum with rolled-in lifters · helix liner (screws food out) ·
abrasive liner (peeling) · basket liner (wash, spin, boil-in) · mouth sieve.
Tools on the arm, entering through the mouth: scraper + roller (knead, wipe the wall while pouring) ·
Kutter knives (bowl chopper) · slicing head · whisk · masher · spray lance.
Weak: one drum is a serial bottleneck; flat items need a separate flat station.
1/8 Mouth up (+60°): the tipper dock pours potatoes down the chute into the drum with the abrasive liner.
2/8 Tilt to +15°, 50 rpm: the potatoes tumble on the abrasive wall under the spray lance; peel slurry runs to the gutter.
3/8 Tilt to −35°: the peeled potatoes pour out of the mouth into the pot below.
4/8 Mouth up again: onions in; the Kutter knives enter through the mouth while the drum turns slowly — even chopping.
5/8 Tilt to +15°: the drum's own induction coil heats the wall; the onions tumble-fry like in a rotating wok.
6/8 Tilt to −35°: the fried onions pour into the pan.
7/8 Self-wash: 1.5 L water heated by the coil to 55 °C, tumbling with lance jet; then poured into the gutter.
8/8 Spin at 450 rpm throws off the water film, then the empty drum heats itself to 110 °C: dry and disinfected.
